title: Lost Things Turn Up
dateline: The bell tower. The last week.
mood: On the bell tower at night, Selena counts what she has seen this year and keeps every secret.

hero.alt: In a bright classroom Selena grins as she holds up her drawing, red-haired Fanny laughs beside her with a V sign, and pink-haired Angela leans in from the right to look.

segs.t: Selena lay on her stomach at the edge of the tiles, chin on her folded arms, a lollipop stick at the corner of her mouth. Silverbolt lay curled against her side. The night was clear.
Across the grounds, at the top of the Academy’s tower, the observation lab was lit. Behind the glass a telescope crept along the sky. Under the lamp, a pink ponytail hung over the eyepiece.
Past the dome’s landward edge, the dead ground was black. On a rise out there, a ruined tower with no roof stood against the stars. Nothing showed on it tonight. Once, something had.
And over the bay, past the dome’s seaward edge, hung a faint point of light.
It had come out this week, where there had never been a star. On Chang’e’s screens it would not hold still.
“Every reading runs off the scale right there,” Chang’e had said, tapping the glass. “That’s a singularity.”
Nobody knew what it was. By morning the students were calling it the Singularity.
It was too faint and too far out to fight, so the Academy only watched it. On the cliff above the water, the watch lamps had doubled.
The pull in Selena’s cells came from somewhere near it. She had not mentioned that to Chang’e.
She looked down instead, at the top of the wall she had walked along, late, on the day the transfer came.
By the time she reached the VR Battlefield, a new name topped the board. FANNY, 3:39. Under it, knocked to second: LAYLA, 3:41.
Layla walked out with her chin up and her mouth shut. Selena laughed so hard she sat down on Silverbolt.
The day the dome tore in the northeast, she watched from these tiles. Black Enders came out of an orange sky into the breach. Their hum reached her bones across the city.

At one end Layla’s cannon flashed white, and Fanny swung through the Enders on a cable, blades lit. At the other, Guinevere punched them out of the air, and Vexana’s staff struck down anything that came at her from behind.
Research,
Selena told herself. She stayed until the last Ender fell.

One dawn she came home from a storm run with rain still in her hair. Karina sat at the table in her boots, a cup in both hands. Selena’s door stood open. Her bed lay made, the way she had left it at dusk.
Karina looked at the bed, then at her. Then she drank her tea.
Selena went to school anyway, late. At the attendance desk the clerk frowned at his tablet.
“Your guardian called first thing. A fever.” He looked her up and down. “You look fine.”
“It broke,” said Selena.
She saw the bed,
she thought, all the way up the stairs.
In class she slept on her arms until Layla’s paper plane hit her head and ended a dream about a cupcake. Then she showed her suit design.
Fanny leaned in from the next desk to look at the joints, and her face lit up. Selena was grinning before she had picked a smile. She had no word for that.
Angela crossed the room with her doll to look, and said nothing.
On the stairs a boy called her dangerous. She waved her lollipop over her shoulder and promised him he’d meet the real her one day.
Every word of it true,
she thought.
Go on. Laugh.
The whole stairwell laughed. Guinevere, a few steps behind with Vexana, laughed loudest, her head thrown back. Selena liked that too.
At supper that night Karina passed her the bread. “Cellars flooded in the old market. We got them all out.”
She never said the word fever. Neither did Selena.
Later, in Chang’e’s lab, they bet on a knee joint of Selena’s.
“It’ll crack,” said Chang’e.
“Two puddings says it won’t.”
The test press climbed past the mark. The joint held.
Selena held out both hands. “Hehe, I win again!”
Chang’e pushed the puddings across one at a time and sighed over each.
Halfway through the first, Selena’s phone flashed red on the bench. The pull came with it.
“And we were having such a nice mood.” Selena said it to the phone, and swiped the message away unread.
At the next bench, where Angela sat each week for her check, Ruby looked up. “You didn’t even read it.”
“Never do.”
Ruby smiled at her as if she had pulled a coin out of the air. After that Ruby said good morning to her every day. Selena never found out why.
Across the grounds, the telescope crept along again. It had started after Vexana was taken.
The news had come down the halls with the sirens still going. A door had opened inside the Academy’s walls, and an Ender had taken Vexana through it.
By evening the board outside the Combat office said VEXANA: MISSING, in the same type as a roster. Guinevere stood in front of it with two fingers at her collar.
Selena stopped at the far end of the hall.
A door in here,
she thought.
They don’t open doors in here. Not unless they want something badly.
She went on to the lab.
Now she looked toward the ruined tower.
Not long after the board went up, a girl had stepped out of the dark into her lamp at the crews’ yard.
Her black hair had gone blue-lavender, magenta at the tips. Horns rose out of it, real ones. Selena knew real ones. The girl wore an Ender’s robe and carried a staff with a black orb.
The missing ace had gone over. In shape, anyway: she had waited in the dark for the big man to leave. An Ender would not have waited.
“Nice hair,” was all she had said about it.
She openly sold Ender technology recovered from wreckage to Vexana, curious to see how another pawn like herself might escape the game.
Openly, because the girl could not tell on her without telling on herself. And she paid in places: whole Enders lying where no crew had been yet. That beat money.
“Most of them think you’re dead,” Selena had said over the sack. “Your partner doesn’t.” She had said it only to watch the face.
Vexana’s face did not move. Her left hand went halfway to her right sleeve and stopped. Selena saw both. She liked her better for the face.

Some mornings later in Chang’e’s lab, Ruby had code running, and Angela held a small gold star in both cupped hands. Guinevere stood over them with her arms folded. Her bow was crooked. All year it had been straight.
Selena passed the bench with a lollipop in her cheek and Silverbolt clicking at her heel. She looked at the star.
“Lost things turn up,” she said, to nobody.
She was out the door before anyone answered.
That one was free,
she thought.
The first sack had held a knee and a shoulder. Vexana came back on other nights for more: the other knee and a thigh, then two forearms and a hip. Then she asked for cores.
“Cores cost extra,” Selena had told her. “Three places each.”
Four came over the weeks, cracked across. A suit took one core. Selena never asked what the other three were for.

One storm night, crossing the dead ground from a ditch she had been paid with, she looked up at the ruined tower. Lightning lit it white. On the top floor stood a figure with a staff, long hair blowing, facing the city. Facing the Academy.
The next flash showed only broken stone.
One morning she rode in under the courtyard billboard of the two girls back to back. Guinevere stood below it, looking up at the black-haired girl, her hand at her collar. She did not look round.
Selena had not heard her laugh since the corridor.
Two words would do it,
she thought.
Dead ground.
She rode past.
On the tower, Selena sat up. In the lit glass the telescope had turned a little farther.
She tilted her lollipop at that window. Then she tilted it past the dome, at the ruined tower in the dark.
Not a word,
she thought.
To either of you.
Over the bay, the faint point hung where it had all week. The pull came again from near it. Nearer than last night.
